text:
Chapter Eleven


The next morning, Rory and Simon returned at an hour that Arthur could only describe as horridly early. In fact, if pressed, he would have said it was the middle of the night, actually. There was barely a hint in the sky that dawn was approaching, but at least the overly strong coffee that their father liked to brew was percolating away. In the near darkness, a bleary Arthur filled a mug halfway with cream and leaned against the counter, waiting for the coffee to finish brewing. Rory barely said a word to him, his eyes practically closed at the table as he tried to persuade Simon to stop bouncing from side to side and eat his toast.


Barry emerged from his room wearing his fishing vest, stinking like decades-old seawater and remnants of fish guts. “Ready, kiddo?” Barry shouted, and Arthur and Rory groaned while Simon whooped.


“I need everyone to speak several decibels quieter,” Rory said.


Simon bounced on his tiptoes and asked his next question in a theatrical whisper. “What can we catch today, Poppy?”


Barry ignored Rory’s plea and spoke in his normal, booming voice. “I listened to the fish report when I woke up, and they’re catching flounder and bluefish in the cove.”


“Flounder!” Simon screeched at a pitch a dog would struggle to hear, and Rory glared at his father. “Uncle Artie, have you ever seen a flounder? They look so weird. One time, I caught a flounder as long as Poppy’s arm, and he said it was the biggest he’s ever seen.”


When Arthur had been small, his father had sometimes taken him out fishing early in the morning before he went to work and Arthur went to summer camp on the beach, his hair and skin smelling like salt, sand, and sunscreen for weeks at a time. He was fairly certain his father had told him he’d caught the biggest flounder Barry had ever seen, but Arthur supposed he could concede the record to his nephew.


“We’re not going to catch a thing if we don’t skedaddle,” Barry said, clipping his keys to his vest and gathering a handful of sparkling fake tadpoles from a clear container that he kept unfortunately close to the cooking ingredients. He held one in his hand and whispered a Diadhan word that Arthur didn’t quite catch, tossing the fake tadpole to Simon, who squealed when it wriggled in his hand like a living thing, glittering as if it had caught a sunbeam. “New at the bait shop! Looks real, doesn’t it?” Barry explained. “See how it’s bright with its own light?”


“Show him on the boat, Pop.” Rory yawned as he zipped up Simon’s lime-green life jacket. Down on his son’s level, he scruffed up Simon’s hair and kissed him on the cheek. “Listen to Poppy,” he reminded the boy, handing him a tube of sunscreen. “Stay in the boat. I don’t care that you’re wearing a life jacket. Do not jump in. And make sure Poppy takes you out to lunch. I don’t want to see you back here until two o’clock, at the earliest.” Rory gave their father a pointed look to make sure he understood those words were really for him, and Barry gave him a thumbs-up behind the boy’s head.


Simon leaned into Rory and whispered loudly and knowingly, “Because you have to help Uncle Artie with his problem.”


Rory glanced over at Arthur with an apology in his grimace. “That’s right,” he said, planting a kiss on the boy’s head as the three of them walked out the door. The stars were only just beginning to wink out as Rory buckled Simon into the truck and then said something to Barry, who nodded and waved off his younger son.


Arthur hadn’t told Rory much last night before he went home. Just that he needed some advice. And then he’d casually said the one phrase that he knew would get Rory to drop everything: about a woman at work. Fortunately, the already-planned fishing trip gave them the perfect excuse to spend the day together, but now that Barry and Simon were pulling out of the driveway and Rory was returning to the living room, Arthur was faced with having to tell him everything about what had happened. All he wanted to do was return to his too-small bed.


As the front door slammed, Arthur grumbled, “I’m going back to sleep.” They could discuss Maggie at a reasonable hour.


Rory grabbed his shoulder and turned him around, pushing him down onto Barry’s old corduroy couch. Rory claimed Pop’s chair so he could sit across from Arthur. “We don’t have time for sleep,” his brother said. “I’m pretty sure you’ve never once asked for my advice, so things must be bad. We’re going to need every minute between now and two.” There was a preening, self-satisfied look on Rory’s face that almost made Arthur smile despite his exhaustion. For the first time since the pall fell, he felt a wave of calm wash over him. Rory may be his little brother, but giving someone else the reins was all Arthur wanted right now. Let someone else figure out this mess he’d found himself in.


The last five years of parenthood had aged his little brother, though to Arthur he still looked so young. He always wondered if people could tell they were siblings. They both had brown hair, with enough grays that it was noticeable, but Arthur favored his mother and the rest of the Taliesins in most other ways. His skin was her same milky pale, while Rory tanned easily. Arthur was tall, with gangly limbs even as he’d grown soft in adulthood, while Rory was shorter with a broad, muscular build.


Of course, anyone who knew both Arthur and Rory was more likely to compare their personalities. Rory was charming. He had an army of friends, people he’d met at every stage of life, many of whom had stepped up to help him with Simon over the past few years. Arthur, on the other hand, had been so single-minded and focused on his research that he hadn’t had time to maintain the easy friendships of college. The moment he had been accepted into Dartwood’s alchemical doctorate program, notoriously competitive and demanding, the rest fell away. Sure, there had been people in his labs that he liked, that he might consider friends if he weren’t their boss, but he always kept a very appropriate distance between himself and his employees and colleagues. And since most of his time had been spent in his lab, he rarely had a chance to meet someone who didn’t fall into one of those two categories. It was lonely.


“Do we have time for breakfast?” Arthur asked as he finished the last of his coffee.


“Later. After you tell me everything.”


Arthur tried to swallow his nerves. He didn’t want to tell Rory everything. He hadn’t mentioned the pall or what happened that day to cause it. What good would come out of it? Rory would probably be furious about the way he had been putting himself in danger to try to dissipate the pall. Worse, Rory would probably tell him that it wasn’t his fault, when it most decidedly was.


After a few false starts—it just felt so unnatural to admit to his baby brother that he was floundering—he told Rory about how he met the woman on Beltane. He told him how he had been so confident and so not himself that he hadn’t known what witchcraft had come over him. He told him how electric it had been to kiss her as they danced, as the bonfires burned around them and the gods begged for fire, for love, for lust.


And then he told him about the small basement office he’d been sharing with his prickly colleague—“Pricklier than you?” Rory interjected and Arthur ignored him—who seemed to hate him for reasons he didn’t understand.


But he didn’t tell him about the magic he shouldn’t have done, much too intricate for his undergraduate students. And he didn’t tell him how he had messed up that spell, all because he’d been distracted. Instead, he told him how a single touch of the softest skin at Maggie’s wrist had been enough to break the spell the mask had cast over his memory.


Rory was quiet, and Arthur fidgeted, rubbing the palm of his hand over the worn corduroy ridges of the couch. When he finally spoke, Rory’s voice carried a mixture of awe and annoyance. “First of all, I can’t believe you didn’t tell me about Beltane.” Arthur had ripped off his mask the second he’d walked through the dunes and returned to the truck so that he wouldn’t have to tell his brother the truth of what had happened.


“There was nothing to tell!” Arthur insisted. “As far as I knew, she was a stranger I’d never see again, and even if I did, I wasn’t supposed to recognize her. It wasn’t supposed to be Maggie.” Arthur buried his face in his hands. “What am I going to do, Rory?”


“What do you want to do?”


“I should tell her the truth. That’s the right thing to do. But how do you tell your coworker, ‘We have absolutely had our tongues down each other’s throats and, oh, by the way, I’ve known for days’?”


“Maybe leave that last part off,” Rory suggested unhelpfully.


“She’s never going to speak to me again.” Arthur knew he sounded ridiculous and whiny, but he couldn’t be normal about this. Not about that kiss. Not about Maggie.


Rory rolled his eyes. “And if she finds out you knew and you kept it from her? What will she think of you then?”


Arthur should make himself do the right thing, but he was selfish. He wanted to do whatever would make Maggie hate him the least. He just didn’t know what that was. He wasn’t fool enough to think that Maggie would ever like him, but at least she might not hate him quite so much. Rory watched him thoughtfully, like he was turning over Arthur’s problem in his mind. “How exactly do you think that rune worked?”


“Hang on,” Arthur said and disappeared into his bedroom. He returned a moment later with the mask in hand, holding it carefully to prevent damaging the delicate drying blooms.


Rory looked at Arthur like he didn’t recognize him. “You kept it? That must have been some kiss,” he said, incredulous. “Oh, you’re screwed, Artie.”


“Thank you, but I already knew that.”


Rory took the mask from Arthur, holding it as gently as his brother had, and turned it over until he found the complicated rune. Working out a spell’s intention backward from its rune was tricky, but not impossible. It was much easier and more accurate if you knew the Diadhan incantation that powered the rune, but even without it, there was plenty you could glean from the line work.


Arthur shuffled through Barry’s belongings for some paper. He copied the lines of the rune, an approximation of the spell at a larger size. “This’ll be the time line,” Arthur said, annotating the part of the rune that dated the spell for Beltane night. “But this…” Arthur pointed to where the lines of the rune twisted around each other. “Do you recognize any of this?”


Rory shook his head but then pointed out another spot he did recognize. “These are the memory lines. I’ve seen the same ones on runes at work, but those are meant to keep something in your memory, to make it easier to remember important trail markers.” Rory, like their dad, was a park ranger. Though he had never been as interested in the science of magic as Arthur was, he used his fair share in the field.


“That doesn’t tell us anything we don’t already know about the spell,” Arthur grumbled. He remembered the woman who had handed them their masks with a wink and a not-so-subtle glance at Rory that his brother had ignored. Was she the one who created the spell? “It must be in the incantation.”


“What else do we know? What happened the exact moment you remembered?”


Arthur closed his eyes, remembering how the pad of his finger had barely grazed the skin at her wrist. Just like it had when he’d turned her wrist over in his hand to look at the burn the ghoul had left. Just like it had when he’d saved Maggie from falling down the stairs…and neither of those times had cleared the static. Neither of those moments had been enough to break the spell. “I think I got it wrong,” he said, thinking out loud. “I’ve touched her wrist before, shaken her hand before, but it was never enough to unlock my memories.”


“If that wasn’t it, what was? What was different this time?”


As he had danced with Maggie beneath the stars, Arthur had stroked the small divot where her palm met her wrist, but that wasn’t the first time they’d touched. The first time was when she’d reached her hand out to help him off the sand. It was when she’d asked him in that bold voice to get her a drink, with that fire in her eyes, reflecting the living flame of the bonfires all around them. Then, in their office, to seal their agreement, there had been that same expression.


Oh. Both times, Maggie had invited him into her life with a single gesture, with a little bit of trust and a little bit of a dare. A challenge. Both times, he had engulfed her smaller hand in his, marveling at the way it fit, at the way he wanted to live up to whatever challenge she saw before her. It wasn’t the touch at all. It was what it meant.


After Arthur explained this revelation to Rory, his brother clapped his hands together. “Then that’s your answer,” Rory said, as if it were obvious what Arthur should do.


“What is?”


“You just need to figure out what that same moment was for Maggie and help her remember.”


Arthur looked at his brother incredulously. “You can’t be serious.”


“If you both remember…”


“I’m not going to lie to her.”


“Who said anything about lying! Just try. For a week. If you can get her to remember in a few days, you can say you were working up the courage to tell her. Which is true, by the way.”


He had no idea if there was anything about that night that would have stood out to Maggie. Was it when they pressed their bodies together and swayed to the music? Or something simpler? When his hand cradled her chin before their kiss? What if it was when he made her laugh? Arthur could never try to be funny. Everything would definitely come crashing down.


“This is a terrible plan.” What was he supposed to do? Pretend to trip and crash into her lips? Maybe he could persuade her to go over their notes at a bar instead of Bean There, Done That so he could buy her a drink. It was an absurd plan. And Arthur certainly wasn’t going to kiss her without telling her the truth first. Gods below, he was going to have to figure out how to tell a damn joke.


“What kind of deal did you make with her, anyway? Did she draw a line down the middle of your office and make you promise you won’t cross it?”


Arthur had walked himself into this corner. How could he talk about their bargain without explaining the monster of a pall? Arthur was a terrible liar, he knew that, so he told Rory an approximation of the truth. “There’s a pall on campus and we’re having trouble getting rid of it. We made a deal so Maggie can help with its removal.” And then he couldn’t quite stop himself from talking about it more. He didn’t deserve to feel relief, but between Maggie’s help and the concern etched in Rory’s forehead, he felt it all the same. “I’ve never seen a pall like this one, Ror. Our dissipation spells just aren’t working.”


His first attempt at a dissipation had fizzled to nothing in front of his eyes, the lines of his rune glowing with promising power until they burned out with a pop, sending up a cloud of the gold dust that infused his chalk until the air shimmered. His second attempt had been no better, and when, on the third attempt, a piercing crack had shaken the floor, Arthur had braced himself for the pall to grow larger and consume more of Ilex Hall. Fortunately, it had just grown soupier, but he was fully traumatized by the event.


Magic had never confounded him like this. He’d learned early on that if he just kept working on a spell, eventually he’d understand it. Persistence was better than any genius, especially in an alchemy lab. Even when magic took time, took trial and error, there was always measurable progress and eventually success. Magic was supposed to be the easy thing. People were hard. Relationships impossible. But magic? That he understood. He was on the verge of falling into another spiral about the pall, when Rory hummed in thought, oblivious to the way Arthur’s mind was spinning nearly out of control.


“I don’t know much about getting rid of a pall, but you know that magic can get strange so close to the Wilds. Maybe your answer is there?”


Arthur considered the possibility, then his phone buzzed. The way his brother’s eyes lit up was his only warning as he lunged for it. Rory just managed to grab the phone before Arthur did, flipping open the screen and holding it just out of Arthur’s reach.


“You’re thirty-three years old, Rory,” Arthur grumbled. “Give me my phone back.”


Rory sighed. “It’s just Pop. Look at this gigantic fish Simon caught.” Rory flipped the phone around and showed Arthur the photo of a beaming Simon holding a huge flounder, the sky rosy pink with dawn behind him. Underneath the photo was a message Arthur was sure his father had typed while he tried to wrangle another piece of bait on Simon’s line: Send this to Ror.


“Why does he do that?”


“You know he always just texts whoever messaged him last instead of typing in our name.”


Arthur rolled his eyes, getting up to finally find something to eat.


As he rummaged through the fridge for some jam, Rory groaned and muttered a curse under his breath. “Oops,” he said, a little louder. Arthur closed the fridge door slowly and turned to see Rory frantically typing on the phone screen.


“ ‘Oops’? Oops what?”


“I think I accidentally sent it to Maggie?” Arthur closed his eyes slowly. “I didn’t know you were texting her! You conveniently left that out of your story earlier!”


Arthur tried not to panic. “It is six thirty in the morning. You did not just send her a photo of a fish at six thirty in the morning.” The grimace on Rory’s face was comically large, but that did not make Arthur feel better.


“Well, I mean, it’s a picture of Simon with a fish, so…”


“Does that make it better?” Arthur asked, exasperated.


“Objectively, yes, it would be so much weirder if you just sent her a picture of a fish.”


Arthur wanted to throw something at his brother. He marveled at the calm he felt just moments ago at having Rory helping him. All gone. Brothers. “I’m going back to bed.”

facts.fact: 清晨六点半 Barry 带 Simon 出海钓比目鱼；Simon 尖声+大声耳语「帮 Uncle Artie 解决 problem」。
Rory 就任军师：Arthur 从没求过他一次建议——所以 must be bad；两 点前每分钟都要用。
facts.anchor: never once asked for my advice

facts.fact: Arthur 全盘托出 Beltane：自信得不像自己、被巫术附体；共舞之吻「来电」。
facts.anchor: what witchcraft had come over him

facts.fact: 他一进沙丘回卡车就扯掉面具——为的是不告诉弟弟真相。
facts.anchor: ripped off his mask the second

facts.fact: 符文拆解：Rory 认出 memory lines（护林员经验）；施法者疑指发面具时冲 Rory 眨眼的女人。
关键推理：之前摸腕握手都没解锁——触发条件不是触碰。
facts.anchor: it was never enough to unlock my memories

facts.fact: 真因：两次解锁都发生在她「信任+挑衅」的邀请手势时刻——是意义不是触碰。
Rory 处方：找到那一刻对 Maggie 的对应物、帮她也想起来；一星期内成功能说你在鼓起勇气。
消散咒三连败：金尘烧穿 pop、第二次无起色、第三次地板裂 pall 变汤——魔法他懂的信仰裂缝。
Wilds 线索：魔法在 Wilds 附近会变怪；随后 Barry 误把鱼照发进 Arthur 与 Maggie 的对话框。
